rationale: The student mistakenly adds the denominators together (getting tenths instead of fifths). A number line divided into fifths visually demonstrates that adding fifths means taking steps of size 1/5 along the fifths line, keeping the denominator constant while only counting up the numerators.

script.focus: The size of each tick mark stays 1/5, so adding hops counts fifths rather than changing the denominator.

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: The size of each tick mark stays 1/5, so adding hops counts fifths rather than changing the denominator.

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The student erroneously added denominators (getting 3/10 for 2/5 + 1/5). The demo switches from a fraction bar to a number line, explicitly demonstrating that hops along fifths simply count how many fifths there are without changing the denominator size (1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5). It is passive/worked (easier), uses a distinct visual representation, and directly targets why the denominator remains 5.
judgement.verdict: A teacher would definitely use this demo to clearly show on a number line that hopping fifths counts parts while keeping the denominator unchanged.
